If the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [GDPR, Article 33(1)].

q02.question: Is a company that buys an AI tool from a vendor and uses it internally a 'provider' or a 'deployer' under the AI Act?
q02.answer:
A company that buys an AI tool from a vendor and uses it under its authority is a 'deployer', provided it is not used for a personal non-professional activity [AI Act, Article 3(4)]. A 'provider' is instead a person or body that develops the AI system or has it developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark [AI Act, Article 3(2)].

q03.question: Can we use AI software to detect our employees' emotions during video calls?
q03.answer:
No, you cannot use AI systems to infer the emotions of your employees during video calls, as the use of AI systems to infer emotions in the area of the workplace is prohibited [AI Act, Article 5(1)]. The only exception is when such a system is intended to be put in place or into the market strictly for medical or safety reasons [AI Act, Article 5(1)].

q04.question: Can a provider argue that an AI system on the high-risk list is not actually high-risk?
q04.answer:
Yes, a provider can consider that an AI system listed in Annex III is not high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, provided it meets specific conditions such as performing a narrow procedural task or improving a previously completed human activity [AI Act, Article 6(3)]. However, the provider must document this assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, is subject to a registration obligation, and must provide the documentation upon request from national competent authorities [AI Act, Article 6(4)]. Note that an AI system always remains high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons [AI Act, Article 6(3)].

q05.question: What qualities does the AI Act require of the data used to train a high-risk AI system?
q05.answer:
The AI Act requires that training, validation, and testing data sets be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose [AI Act, Article 10(2), 10(3)]. They must also have appropriate statistical properties, including regarding the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used [AI Act, Article 10(3)]. Furthermore, data sets must take into account the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting where the system will be used [AI Act, Article 10(4)].

q06.question: What must a person overseeing a high-risk AI system be able to do?
q06.answer:
Natural persons assigned to oversee a high-risk AI system must be enabled to understand its capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, and detect anomalies or unexpected performance [AI Act, Article 14(4)]. They must remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the system's outputs, and decide not to use the system or override its output in any particular situation [AI Act, Article 14(4)]. They must also be able to intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it using a 'stop' button or similar procedure that brings it to a safe state [AI Act, Article 14(4)].

q07.question: We use a high-risk AI system bought from a vendor. What are our main obligations as the company using it?
q07.answer:
As a deployer of a high-risk AI system, you must use the system in accordance with its accompanying instructions for use, assign competent and trained natural persons to ensure human oversight, and ensure that any input data under your control is relevant and sufficiently representative [AI Act, Article 26(1)-(4)]. You must also monitor the system's operation, keep its automatically generated logs under your control for at least six months (unless otherwise provided by law), and suspend use and inform the provider and authorities without undue delay if you suspect the system presents a risk or causes a serious incident [AI Act, Article 26(5)-(6)].

q16.question: Can we make decisions about customers purely with an algorithm, with no human involved?
q16.answer:
Customers have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them [GDPR, Article 22(1)]. When based on a contract or explicit consent, the controller must implement suitable measures to safeguard the customer's rights, including at least the right to obtain human intervention, express their point of view, and contest the decision [GDPR, Article 22(3)].

q17.answer:

q18.question: Does the maker of a smart connected device have to give users access to the data the device generates?
q18.answer:
Yes, connected products must be designed and manufactured so that their data and related metadata are directly accessible to the user by default, securely, free of charge, and in a structured, machine-readable format [Data Act, Article 3(1)]. If the data cannot be directly accessed from the product, the data holder must make the data accessible to the user without undue delay, of the same quality, and free of charge [Data Act, Article 4(1)]. Sellers or lessors, which may include the manufacturer, must also provide clear information beforehand on how the user may access, retrieve, or erase the data [Data Act, Article 3(2)].

q21.answer:
A data-access or data-use contractual term that has been unilaterally imposed by one enterprise on another is not binding if it is unfair [Data Act, Article 13(1)]. However, a term is not considered unfair if it simply reflects mandatory Union law or provisions that would apply anyway [Data Act, Article 13(2)].

q25.question: What human involvement do the GDPR and the AI Act require when a system makes decisions about people?
q25.answer:
Under the GDPR, individuals have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing—including profiling—that produce legal or similarly significant effects, unless exceptions apply such as explicit consent or contract necessity [GDPR, Article 22(1)-(2)]. Where those exceptions apply, the controller must implement suitable measures giving the data subject the right to obtain human intervention, express their point of view, and contest the decision [GDPR, Article 22(3)]. 

Under the AI Act, high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to enable effective human oversight by natural persons to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights [AI Act, Article 14(1)-(2)]. Deployers must assign human oversight to competent, trained individuals equipped to understand the system's limitations, guard against automation bias, interpret outputs, and override, reverse, or stop the system when necessary [AI Act, Article 14(4), Article 26(2)].
